text: The anterior 2/3 of the tongue is derived from the {{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch.
extraInfo: General sensation is provided by V3 (lingual nerve).

text: The posterior 1/3 of the tongue is derived from the {{c1::3rd and 4th}} pharyngeal arches.
extraInfo: Sensation and taste are provided by CN IX.

text: Taste sensation to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue is provided by the {{c1::chorda tympani (CN VII)}}.
extraInfo: It hitches a ride with the lingual nerve (V3).

text: Most tongue muscles are derived from {{c1::occipital somites}} and are innervated by {{c2::CN XII}}.
extraInfo: Exception: Palatoglossus (CN X).

text: The only tongue muscle innervated by the Vagus nerve (CN X) is the {{c1::palatoglossus}}.
extraInfo: All other muscles are innervated by CN XII.

text: A lesion of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) causes the tongue to deviate {{c1::toward}} the side of the lesion.
extraInfo: 'Lick your wounds.' This is due to the unopposed action of the contralateral genioglossus.

text: The foramen cecum on the tongue is the embryological remnant of the {{c1::thyroglossal duct}}.
extraInfo: It marks the site of origin for the thyroid gland.

text: The most common tracheoesophageal anomaly, occurring in ~85% of cases, is {{c1::esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula}}.
extraInfo: This is known as Type C.

text: In a neonate with esophageal atresia, the presence of air in the stomach on X-ray indicates the presence of a {{c1::distal tracheoesophageal fistula}}.
extraInfo: Air travels from the trachea through the fistula into the distal esophagus and stomach.

text: Tracheoesophageal fistulae are often associated with the VACTERL association, where 'C' stands for {{c1::cardiac}} defects and 'R' stands for {{c2::renal}} anomalies.
extraInfo: VACTERL: Vertebral, Anal, Cardiac, TEF, Renal, Limb.

text: The H-type tracheoesophageal fistula, which presents without atresia, is also known as {{c1::Type E}}.
extraInfo: It often presents later with recurrent pneumonia and cyanosis during feeds.

text: Pure esophageal atresia (Type A) is characterized by a {{c1::gasless}} abdomen on X-ray.
extraInfo: Since there is no fistula to the distal GI tract, no air can enter the stomach.

text: The prenatal finding of {{c1::polyhydramnios}} is common in esophageal atresia because the fetus cannot swallow {{c2::amniotic fluid}}.
extraInfo: Failure of GI absorption leads to excess fluid in the amniotic sac.

text: A classic clinical sign of esophageal atresia in a newborn is {{c1::drooling}}, {{c2::choking}}, and {{c3::cyanosis}} with the first feeding.
extraInfo: The inability to pass a nasogastric tube confirms the diagnosis.

text: The physiological herniation of the midgut occurs during the {{c1::6th}} week of development.
extraInfo: This occurs through the umbilical ring into the umbilical cord.

text: The midgut returns to the abdominal cavity during the {{c1::10th}} week of development.
extraInfo: Failure to return results in an omphalocele.

text: The midgut rotates a total of {{c1::270}} degrees {{c2::counterclockwise}} around the superior mesenteric artery.
extraInfo: This occurs in two stages (90 degrees then 180 degrees).

text: The embryonic midgut is supplied by the {{c1::superior mesenteric artery}}.
extraInfo: The celiac artery supplies the foregut, and the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut.

text: The midgut extends from the distal duodenum to the {{c1::proximal two-thirds}} of the transverse colon.
extraInfo: The junction between the midgut and hindgut is a common watershed area for ischemia.

text: The epithelial lining of the gastrointestinal tract is derived from {{c1::endoderm}}.
extraInfo: The smooth muscle and connective tissue are derived from splanchnic mesoderm.

text: Unlike gastroschisis, an omphalocele is covered by {{c1::peritoneum and amnion}}.
extraInfo: Omphalocele is a midline defect, whereas gastroschisis is usually paraumbilical.

text: Congenital umbilical hernia is caused by the failure of the {{c1::umbilical ring}} to close after the return of the midgut.
extraInfo: This occurs at the site of the linea alba.

text: Unlike omphalocele, a congenital umbilical hernia is covered by {{c1::normal skin and subcutaneous tissue}}.
extraInfo: In omphalocele, the herniated bowel is covered by a sac of peritoneum and amnion.

text: Congenital umbilical hernias are strongly associated with {{c1::Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)}}.
extraInfo: Other associations include congenital hypothyroidism and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

text: The management of choice for most infants with a congenital umbilical hernia is {{c1::observation (spontaneous closure)}}.
extraInfo: Most hernias close on their own by age 5 as the rectus muscles grow.

text: Surgical repair for a congenital umbilical hernia is generally indicated if the defect persists beyond age {{c1::5}}.
extraInfo: Surgery may be indicated earlier if the hernia is extremely large or becomes incarcerated.

text: An infant with an umbilical hernia, macroglossia, and neonatal hypoglycemia should be evaluated for {{c1::Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome}}.
extraInfo: These patients have an increased risk of Wilms tumor.

text: In a neonate, an umbilical hernia combined with macroglossia and prolonged jaundice suggests {{c1::congenital hypothyroidism}}.
extraInfo: Treatment with levothyroxine is essential to prevent intellectual disability.

text: Gastroschisis is caused by the failure of {{c1::lateral fold}} closure during development.
extraInfo: This results in a paraumbilical defect, usually to the right of the umbilicus, with no covering sac.

text: Omphalocele is caused by the failure of the {{c1::herniated midgut}} to return to the abdominal cavity.
extraInfo: The contents are covered by a sac of peritoneum and amnion.

text: The sac in an omphalocele consists of {{c1::peritoneum}} and {{c2::amnion}}.
extraInfo: Unlike gastroschisis, which has no sac and is not midline.

text: In gastroschisis, the defect is typically located to the {{c1::right}} of the umbilicus.
extraInfo: The umbilical cord insertion is normal and separate from the defect.

text: Omphalocele is frequently associated with {{c1::Trisomies (13, 18, 21)}} and {{c2::Beckwith-Wiedemann}} syndrome.
extraInfo: Gastroschisis is usually an isolated defect.

text: The bowel in gastroschisis often appears matted/thickened due to exposure to {{c1::amniotic fluid}}.
extraInfo: This 'chemical peritonitis' causes delayed intestinal function (ileus) after repair.

text: Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) is {{c1::elevated}} in both gastroschisis and omphalocele.
extraInfo: Levels are generally higher in gastroschisis because the bowel is 'naked'.

text: The classic age of presentation for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is {{c1::2-6 weeks}} of life.
extraInfo: It rarely presents at birth because the hypertrophy of the pylorus is a progressive postnatal process.

text: The acid-base and electrolyte profile of a patient with HPS is {{c1::hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis}}.
extraInfo: This is due to loss of HCl and secondary hyperaldosteronism leading to renal K+ and H+ loss.

text: The pathognomonic physical exam finding in hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is an {{c1::olive-shaped}} mass in the epigastrium.
extraInfo: It is best felt immediately after the infant has vomited.

text: Exposure to {{c1::macrolides (e.g., erythromycin)}} is a known pharmacological risk factor for the development of HPS.
extraInfo: Macrolides are motilin receptor agonists, which may trigger pyloric hypertrophy.

text: The vomitus in hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is classically {{c1::non-bilious}} and {{c2::projectile}}.
extraInfo: Non-bilious because the obstruction is proximal to the entry of the common bile duct.

text: The first-line imaging modality for diagnosing HPS is {{c1::ultrasound}}.
extraInfo: Diagnosis is confirmed by a pyloric muscle thickness > 3-4 mm.

text: Before surgical correction of HPS, the clinician must first {{c1::correct fluid and electrolyte imbalances}}.
extraInfo: This reduces the risk of post-operative anesthetic complications like apnea.

text: The pancreas is derived from the {{c1::foregut}} endoderm.
extraInfo: It develops from two buds: the dorsal and ventral buds.

text: The spleen is derived from the {{c1::mesoderm}} (specifically within the {{c2::dorsal mesogastrium}}).
extraInfo: Unlike the liver and pancreas, it is not an endodermal outgrowth of the gut tube.

text: Annular pancreas is caused by the abnormal rotation of the {{c1::ventral}} pancreatic bud.
extraInfo: This results in a ring of tissue encircling the 2nd part of the duodenum.

text: The uncinate process of the pancreas is derived from the {{c1::ventral}} pancreatic bud.
extraInfo: The dorsal bud forms the tail, body, and superior head.

text: Pancreas divisum is caused by the failure of the {{c1::dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts}} to fuse.
extraInfo: This occurs during the 8th week of gestation.

text: In pancreas divisum, the majority of the pancreas drains through the {{c1::accessory}} duct (Santorini) into the {{c2::minor}} duodenal papilla.
extraInfo: The ventral duct drains only a small portion into the major papilla.

text: The arterial supply to the spleen is the {{c1::splenic artery}}, which originates from the {{c2::celiac trunk}}.
extraInfo: This reflects the spleen's location in the foregut, despite its mesodermal origin.

text: The hepatoduodenal ligament contains the portal triad: {{c1::Proper hepatic artery}}, {{c1::portal vein}}, and {{c1::common bile duct}}.
The {{c1::splenorenal}} ligament contains the splenic artery, splenic vein, and the {{c2::tail of the pancreas}}.
The falciform ligament contains the {{c1::ligamentum teres hepatis}}, which is a remnant of the fetal {{c2::umbilical vein}}.
The gastrosplenic ligament contains the {{c1::short gastric}} arteries and the {{c2::left gastroepiploic}} vessels.
The gastrocolic ligament, a part of the greater omentum, contains the {{c1::gastroepiploic}} arteries.
The {{c1::ventral}} mesentery gives rise to the falciform, gastrohepatic, and hepatoduodenal ligaments.
The Pringle maneuver involves compression of the {{c1::hepatoduodenal}} ligament to control bleeding from the {{c2::portal triad}}.
Duodenal atresia is caused by a {{c1::failure of recanalization}} of the intestinal lumen.
Jejunal and ileal atresias are caused by {{c1::vascular accidents (ischemia)}} in utero.
The radiographic finding of a {{c1::double bubble}} sign on X-ray is characteristic of duodenal atresia.
Duodenal atresia is strongly associated with {{c1::Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)}}.
An 'apple peel' atresia involves the distal bowel spiraling around the {{c1::ileocolic (or SMA branch)}} artery.
Maternal use of {{c1::cocaine (or tobacco)}} increases the risk of vascular-mediated jejunal atresia.
Polyhydramnios occurs in duodenal atresia because the fetus cannot {{c1::swallow and absorb}} amniotic fluid.
The {{c1::2nd, 3rd, and 4th}} parts of the duodenum are secondary retroperitoneal, while the {{c2::proximal 1st}} part is intraperitoneal.
extraInfo: The duodenal bulb is mobile and can lead to peritonitis if perforated, whereas the retroperitoneal parts lead to retroperitoneal air.

text: The entire pancreas is secondary retroperitoneal except for the {{c1::tail}}, which is {{c2::intraperitoneal}}.
extraInfo: The tail is located within the splenorenal ligament and is at risk during splenectomy.

text: The {{c1::ascending}} and {{c2::descending}} colons are secondary retroperitoneal, whereas the transverse and sigmoid colons are intraperitoneal.
extraInfo: Secondary retroperitoneal structures lose their mesentery during development.

text: Primary retroperitoneal structures include the {{c1::kidneys}}, {{c2::ureters}}, and {{c3::suprarenal (adrenal)}} glands.
extraInfo: These structures develop directly in the retroperitoneum and never have a mesentery.

text: The major abdominal vessels, the {{c1::aorta}} and {{c2::inferior vena cava (IVC)}}, are classified as {{c3::primary retroperitoneal}} structures.
extraInfo: The aorta bifurcates at L4, and the IVC forms at L5.

text: The {{c1::abdominal}} portion of the esophagus is considered a retroperitoneal structure.
extraInfo: This segment is found below the diaphragm (T10 hiatus) and before the cardia of the stomach.

text: In the rectum, the {{c1::lower 1/3::fraction}} is completely retroperitoneal, while the {{c2::upper 1/3::fraction}} is intraperitoneal.
extraInfo: The middle 1/3 is covered by peritoneum only on its anterior surface.

text: The {{c1::Meissner (submucosal)}} plexus is located in the submucosa and controls {{c2::secretion}}.
The muscularis externa of the {{c1::stomach}} contains three layers: {{c2::inner oblique}}, middle circular, and outer longitudinal.
{{c1::Brunner glands}} are found in the submucosa of the {{c2::duodenum}} and secrete {{c3::bicarbonate (alkaline mucus)}}.
{{c1::Peyer patches}} are organized lymphoid aggregates located in the {{c2::submucosa}} and {{c3::lamina propria}} of the {{c4::ileum}}.
The {{c1::Auerbach (myenteric)}} plexus is located between the {{c2::inner circular}} and {{c3::outer longitudinal}} muscle layers of the muscularis externa.
The epithelium of the esophagus is {{c1::nonkeratinized stratified squamous}} and transitions to {{c2::simple columnar}} at the gastroesophageal junction.
The {{c1::pectinate (dentate)}} line is the site where the GI tract epithelium transitions from {{c2::simple columnar}} to {{c3::stratified squamous}}.
The {{c1::Submucosa}} is the GI wall layer that contains the Meissner plexus.
extraInfo: The Meissner plexus (submucosal plexus) controls secretions and blood flow.

text: The Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is located between the {{c1::inner circular}} and {{c2::outer longitudinal}} layers of the muscularis externa.
extraInfo: It primarily regulates GI motility.

text: Brunner glands, which secrete alkaline mucus, are located in the {{c1::submucosa}} of the {{c2::duodenum}}.
extraInfo: They help neutralize gastric acid.

text: In the GI tract, an ulcer is distinguished from an erosion by its extension into the {{c1::submucosa::layer}} or deeper.
extraInfo: Erosions are limited to the mucosa and do not cross the muscularis mucosae.

text: The upper 1/3 of the esophagus contains {{c1::skeletal}} muscle, while the lower 1/3 contains {{c2::smooth}} muscle.
extraInfo: The middle 1/3 is a mix of both types.

text: The pacemakers of the GI tract, known as {{c1::Interstitial cells of Cajal}}, are located in the {{c2::muscularis externa}} layer.
extraInfo: They generate the slow waves or basal electrical rhythm (BER).

text: Intestinal stem cells are located at the base of the {{c1::crypts of Lieberkühn}} in the mucosal layer.
extraInfo: These cells replenish the epithelial lining every few days.

text: The celiac trunk originates from the abdominal aorta at the level of the {{c1::T12}} vertebra.
The three main branches of the celiac trunk are the {{c1::left gastric}}, {{c2::splenic}}, and {{c3::common hepatic}} arteries.
The {{c1::short gastric}} arteries arise from the splenic artery and have no significant anastomoses, making the gastric fundus vulnerable to ischemia.
The {{c1::gastroduodenal}} artery is located posterior to the first part of the duodenum and is a common source of hemorrhage in peptic ulcer disease.
The lesser curvature of the stomach is supplied by the {{c1::left gastric}} and {{c2::right gastric}} arteries.
The greater curvature of the stomach is supplied by the {{c1::left gastro-omental}} and {{c2::right gastro-omental}} arteries.
The celiac trunk supplies embryonic {{c1::foregut}} structures.

topic: Abdominal aorta branches and GI watershed areas
text: The celiac trunk originates from the abdominal aorta at the {{c1::T12}} vertebral level.
extraInfo: This is also the level of the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm.

topic: Abdominal aorta branches and GI watershed areas
text: The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) originates from the abdominal aorta at the {{c1::L1}} vertebral level.
extraInfo: It supplies the midgut and is involved in SMA syndrome (compression of the 3rd part of the duodenum).

topic: Abdominal aorta branches and GI watershed areas
text: The inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) originates from the abdominal aorta at the {{c1::L3}} vertebral level.
extraInfo: It supplies the hindgut, including the descending and sigmoid colon.

topic: Abdominal aorta branches and GI watershed areas
text: The abdominal aorta bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at the {{c1::L4}} vertebral level.
extraInfo: This level corresponds to the superior border of the iliac crests.

topic: Abdominal aorta branches and GI watershed areas
text: The GI watershed area known as the splenic flexure (Griffith's point) is located between the territories of the {{c1::SMA}} and the {{c2::IMA}}.
extraInfo: It is a common site for ischemic colitis during systemic hypotension.

topic: Abdominal aorta branches and GI watershed areas
text: The rectosigmoid junction (Sudek's point) is a watershed area between the {{c1::inferior mesenteric artery (IMA)}} and the {{c2::superior rectal artery}}.
extraInfo: Note: The superior rectal artery is technically the distal branch of the IMA, but this junction remains a vulnerable distal zone.

topic: Abdominal aorta branches and GI watershed areas
text: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome involves compression of the {{c1::third (transverse)}} part of the duodenum between the aorta and the SMA.
extraInfo: Commonly seen in patients with rapid weight loss.

topic: Gastrointestinal blood supply and autonomic innervation
text: The celiac trunk originates from the aorta at the level of {{c1::T12}}.
extraInfo: It supplies the foregut: esophagus to proximal duodenum, including liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and spleen.

topic: Gastrointestinal blood supply and autonomic innervation
text: The {{c1::third (transverse)}} part of the duodenum is compressed in Superior Mesenteric Artery syndrome.
extraInfo: This occurs when the angle between the SMA and the aorta decreases, often due to loss of mesenteric fat.

topic: Gastrointestinal blood supply and autonomic innervation
text: The splenic flexure is a watershed area supplied by the terminal branches of the {{c1::SMA}} and {{c2::IMA}}.
extraInfo: This makes it highly susceptible to ischemic colitis during systemic hypotension.

topic: Gastrointestinal blood supply and autonomic innervation
text: Parasympathetic innervation of the hindgut is provided by the {{c1::pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4)}}.
extraInfo: The hindgut includes the distal 1/3 of the transverse colon to the proximal rectum.

topic: Gastrointestinal blood supply and autonomic innervation
text: The {{c1::short gastric}} arteries are branches of the splenic artery that have poor collateral circulation, making the gastric fundus prone to ischemia.
extraInfo: This is clinically relevant in splenic artery occlusion or during certain gastric surgeries.

topic: Gastrointestinal blood supply and autonomic innervation
text: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is located between the {{c1::inner circular}} and {{c2::outer longitudinal}} muscle layers.
extraInfo: Its primary function is the coordination of gastrointestinal motility (peristalsis).

topic: Gastrointestinal blood supply and autonomic innervation
text: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus primarily regulates {{c1::secretions}} and {{c2::blood flow}} within the GI tract.
extraInfo: It is located within the submucosal layer, just deep to the mucosa.

text: The femoral sheath contains the femoral {{c1::artery}}, femoral {{c1::vein}}, and femoral {{c1::canal}}.
The {{c1::femoral nerve}} is a structure in the femoral triangle that is NOT contained within the femoral sheath.
The femoral sheath is formed by the downward continuation of the {{c1::transversalis}} fascia anteriorly and the {{c1::iliac}} fascia posteriorly.
The most medial compartment of the femoral sheath is the {{c1::femoral canal}}, which contains {{c2::lymphatics (and Cloquet's node)}}.
A femoral hernia is located {{c1::medial}} to the femoral vein.
The superior boundary of the femoral triangle is the {{c1::inguinal ligament}}.
The {{c1::lacunar}} ligament forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring.

topic: Pectinate line anatomy and anal canal pathology
text: The anal canal {{c1::superior}} to the pectinate line is derived from endoderm, while the canal {{c2::inferior}} to the line is derived from ectoderm.
extraInfo: This transition marks the change from hindgut to proctodeum.

topic: Pectinate line anatomy and anal canal pathology
text: Lymphatic drainage superior to the pectinate line goes to the {{c1::internal iliac}} lymph nodes, whereas drainage inferior to the line goes to the {{c2::superficial inguinal}} lymph nodes.
extraInfo: Following the rule that lymphatics follow arterial supply.

topic: Pectinate line anatomy and anal canal pathology
text: Internal hemorrhoids are typically painless because they receive {{c1::visceral (autonomic)}} innervation, while external hemorrhoids are painful because they receive {{c2::somatic (pudendal nerve)}} innervation.
extraInfo: The inferior rectal nerve is the branch of the pudendal nerve involved.

topic: Pectinate line anatomy and anal canal pathology
text: Venous drainage above the pectinate line is via the {{c1::superior rectal}} vein into the {{c2::portal}} system.
extraInfo: Specifically, it drains into the inferior mesenteric vein.

topic: Pectinate line anatomy and anal canal pathology
text: Anal fissures are most commonly found in the {{c1::posterior midline}} and are associated with a {{c2::low-fiber}} diet/constipation.
extraInfo: Lateral fissures should prompt investigation for Crohn's disease or other pathology.

topic: Pectinate line anatomy and anal canal pathology
text: The squamous cell carcinoma of the anus typically occurs {{c1::below}} the pectinate line, while adenocarcinoma occurs {{c2::above}} the line.
extraInfo: Reflects the transition from stratified squamous to columnar epithelium.

topic: Pectinate line anatomy and anal canal pathology
text: In the anal canal, the internal sphincter is composed of {{c1::smooth}} muscle and is {{c2::involuntary}}, while the external sphincter is {{c3::skeletal}} muscle and is {{c4::voluntary}}.
extraInfo: The external sphincter is innervated by S2-S4 via the pudendal nerve.

topic: Liver tissue lobule architecture and hepatic zones
text: The most oxygenated zone of the liver acinus is {{c1::Zone 1 (Periportal zone)}}.

topic: Liver tissue lobule architecture and hepatic zones
text: The liver zone containing the highest concentration of cytochrome P-450 is {{c1::Zone 3 (Pericentral zone)}}.

topic: Liver tissue lobule architecture and hepatic zones
text: The classic hepatic lobule structure has a {{c1::central vein}} at its center and {{c2::portal triads}} at its corners.

topic: Liver tissue lobule architecture and hepatic zones
text: Yellow fever is classically associated with damage to {{c1::Zone 2 (Intermediate zone)}}.

topic: Liver tissue lobule architecture and hepatic zones
text: The zone of the liver most susceptible to ischemia and 'shock liver' is {{c1::Zone 3}}.

topic: Liver tissue lobule architecture and hepatic zones
text: In the liver, blood flows {{c1::centripetally (toward the central vein)}} and bile flows {{c2::centrifugally (toward the portal triad)}}.

topic: Liver tissue lobule architecture and hepatic zones
text: Acetaminophen toxicity causes necrosis primarily in {{c1::Zone 3}} because that is where it is activated to {{c2::NAPQI}}.
The portal-systemic anastomosis at the lower esophagus involves the {{c1::left gastric (coronary)}} vein (portal) and the {{c2::azygos}} vein (systemic).
extraInfo: Dilation of these vessels leads to esophageal varices, which can cause life-threatening hematemesis.

text: Caput medusae results from an anastomosis at the umbilicus between the {{c1::paraumbilical}} veins (portal) and the {{c2::superficial/inferior epigastric}} veins (systemic).
extraInfo: The paraumbilical veins run in the ligamentum teres (remnant of the umbilical vein).

text: The rectal portosystemic anastomosis occurs between the {{c1::superior rectal}} vein (portal) and the {{c2::middle and inferior rectal}} veins (systemic).
extraInfo: This presents clinically as anorectal varices (often described as internal hemorrhoids above the pectinate line).

text: A TIPS procedure connects the {{c1::portal vein}} and the {{c2::hepatic vein}} to reduce portal pressure.
extraInfo: The hepatic vein then drains into the inferior vena cava.

text: Isolated gastric varices in the fundus are highly specific for {{c1::splenic vein}} thrombosis.
extraInfo: This is often a complication of chronic pancreatitis. Blood shunts through the short gastric veins.

text: The portal vein is formed by the union of the {{c1::superior mesenteric vein}} and the {{c2::splenic vein}} behind the neck of the pancreas.
extraInfo: The inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein before the confluence.

text: The major clinical risk of shunting portal blood into the systemic circulation (natural or TIPS) is {{c1::hepatic encephalopathy}}.
extraInfo: This is due to ammonia and other toxins bypassing the liver's detoxification processes.

topic: Biliary tree anatomy and sphincter of Oddi
text: The common bile duct is formed by the union of the {{c1::common hepatic duct}} and the {{c1::cystic duct}}.
extraInfo: The right and left hepatic ducts join to form the common hepatic duct before this junction.

topic: Biliary tree anatomy and sphincter of Oddi
text: The sphincter of Oddi is located in the {{c1::second (or descending)}} part of the duodenum.
extraInfo: It surrounds the major duodenal papilla where the common bile duct and pancreatic duct enter.

topic: Biliary tree anatomy and sphincter of Oddi
text: {{c1::Cholecystokinin (CCK)}} is the hormone that triggers gallbladder contraction and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi.
extraInfo: CCK is produced by I cells in the duodenum and jejunum in response to fats.

topic: Biliary tree anatomy and sphincter of Oddi
text: The cystic artery is most commonly a branch of the {{c1::right hepatic}} artery.
extraInfo: This artery is typically found within the Triangle of Calot during surgery.

topic: Biliary tree anatomy and sphincter of Oddi
text: The spiral valves of {{c1::Heister}} are located in the cystic duct and help maintain its patency.
extraInfo: These folds prevent the duct from collapsing or kinking.

topic: Biliary tree anatomy and sphincter of Oddi
text: Morphine can increase biliary pressure by causing spasm of the {{c1::sphincter of Oddi}}.
extraInfo: This can potentially worsen pain in biliary colic or pancreatitis.

topic: Biliary tree anatomy and sphincter of Oddi
text: In the portal triad, the common bile duct lies {{c1::anterior}} to the portal vein and to the {{c1::right}} of the hepatic artery.
extraInfo: This relationship is crucial for identifying structures in the hepatoduodenal ligament.

text: Indirect inguinal hernias occur {{c1::lateral}} to the inferior epigastric vessels.
extraInfo: They pass through the deep inguinal ring due to a patent processus vaginalis.

text: Direct inguinal hernias occur {{c1::medial}} to the inferior epigastric vessels.
extraInfo: They protrude through Hesselbach's triangle due to transversalis fascia weakness.

text: The femoral hernia protrudes through the femoral canal, which is {{c1::medial}} to the femoral vein.
extraInfo: This hernia type is more common in females and has a high risk of incarceration.

text: The cremasteric muscle and fascia are derived from the {{c1::internal oblique}} muscle.
extraInfo: This is the middle layer of the spermatic cord coverings.

text: In a {{c1::sliding}} hiatal hernia, the gastroesophageal junction is displaced upward into the thorax.
extraInfo: This leads to an 'hourglass stomach' appearance on imaging.

text: A Spigelian hernia occurs through the {{c1::linea semilunaris}} (aponeurosis of the transversus abdominis).
extraInfo: It is usually found at the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle.

text: The inferior border of Hesselbach's triangle is formed by the {{c1::inguinal ligament}}.
extraInfo: Also known as Poupart's ligament.

text: {{c1::Gastrin}} is produced by G cells and acts to increase {{c2::gastric H+ secretion}} and {{c3::gastric mucosal growth}}.
extraInfo: It is stimulated by stomach distension, amino acids, and GRP (vagal). It is inhibited by low pH (< 1.5).

text: Cholecystokinin (CCK) is secreted by {{c1::I cells}} in the duodenum/jejunum and causes {{c2::gallbladder contraction}}, {{c3::pancreatic enzyme secretion}}, and {{c4::relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi}}.
extraInfo: CCK also decreases gastric emptying.

text: {{c1::Secretin}}, released by S cells, stimulates the secretion of {{c2::bicarbonate}} from the pancreas and bile ducts.
extraInfo: It is primarily triggered by acid (H+) in the duodenum.

text: {{c1::Somatostatin}} is produced by D cells and acts as a universal inhibitor, decreasing the secretion of {{c2::all GI hormones}}, gastric acid, and pancreatic juice.
extraInfo: Octreotide is a long-acting analog of somatostatin used to treat acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, and variceal bleeding.

text: Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) is an {{c1::incretin}} produced by K cells that {{c2::increases}} insulin release and {{c3::decreases}} gastric acid secretion.
extraInfo: This is why oral glucose is more effective at raising insulin than IV glucose.

text: {{c1::Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)}} causes profuse {{c2::watery diarrhea}}, {{c3::hypokalemia}}, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome) when secreted by a tumor.
extraInfo: VIP normally causes intestinal smooth muscle relaxation and water/electrolyte secretion.

text: {{c1::Motilin}} is responsible for the Migrating Motor Complexes (MMCs) during the fasting state, and its receptors are stimulated by the antibiotic {{c2::erythromycin}}.
extraInfo: Motilin is secreted by M cells in the small intestine.

topic: Gastrointestinal secretory products and parietal cell physiology
text: The {{c1::parietal}} cells of the stomach are responsible for secreting both hydrochloric acid (HCl) and {{c2::intrinsic factor}}.
extraInfo: Intrinsic factor is essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

topic: Gastrointestinal secretory products and parietal cell physiology
text: Cholecystokinin (CCK) is secreted by {{c1::I cells}} in the duodenum and jejunum, primarily in response to {{c2::fatty acids}} and amino acids.
extraInfo: CCK causes gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion.

topic: Gastrointestinal secretory products and parietal cell physiology
text: Secretin is released from {{c1::S cells}} in the duodenum when the luminal pH is {{c2::low (acidic)}}.
extraInfo: Secretin's main function is to stimulate pancreatic bicarbonate secretion to neutralize the acid.

topic: Gastrointestinal secretory products and parietal cell physiology
text: The universal inhibitor of the GI tract, {{c1::somatostatin::hormone}}, is secreted by {{c2::D cells}} and is stimulated by high gastric acid levels.
extraInfo: Somatostatin inhibits gastrin, secretin, CCK, and insulin release.

topic: Gastrointestinal secretory products and parietal cell physiology
text: The parietal cell H+/K+ ATPase is stimulated by histamine via the {{c1::cAMP}} second messenger pathway and by acetylcholine/gastrin via the {{c2::IP3/Ca2+}} pathway.
extraInfo: This difference in pathways leads to the 'potentiation' of acid secretion.

topic: Gastrointestinal secretory products and parietal cell physiology
text: The 'hunger hormone' {{c1::ghrelin}} is produced by the stomach and increases appetite, while {{c2::leptin}} is produced by adipocytes and signals satiety.
extraInfo: Ghrelin levels are significantly elevated in Prader-Willi syndrome.

topic: Gastrointestinal secretory products and parietal cell physiology
text: {{c1::Brunner glands}} are located in the {{c2::submucosa}} of the duodenum and produce alkaline mucus.
extraInfo: They protect the duodenum from the acidic chyme coming from the stomach.

topic: Inguinal canal layers and spermatic cord
text: The internal spermatic fascia is derived from the {{c1::transversalis fascia}}.
extraInfo: This occurs as the spermatic cord passes through the deep inguinal ring.

topic: Inguinal canal layers and spermatic cord
text: The cremasteric muscle and fascia are derived from the {{c1::internal oblique}} muscle.
extraInfo: This layer provides the motor limb for the cremasteric reflex (genital branch of genitofemoral nerve).

topic: Inguinal canal layers and spermatic cord
text: The external spermatic fascia is derived from the {{c1::external oblique aponeurosis}}.
extraInfo: This layer is acquired at the superficial inguinal ring.

topic: Inguinal canal layers and spermatic cord
text: The {{c1::transversus abdominis}} muscle is the only abdominal wall layer that does NOT contribute a fascia or muscle layer to the spermatic cord.
extraInfo: It does, however, form the roof of the inguinal canal along with the internal oblique.

topic: Inguinal canal layers and spermatic cord
text: An indirect inguinal hernia passes {{c1::lateral}} to the inferior epigastric artery.
extraInfo: This is because it enters through the deep inguinal ring.

topic: Inguinal canal layers and spermatic cord
text: Lymphatic drainage from the testes goes to the {{c1::para-aortic (lumbar)}} lymph nodes.
extraInfo: In contrast, lymph from the scrotum drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.

topic: Inguinal canal layers and spermatic cord
text: The {{c1::ilioinguinal nerve (L1)}} travels through the inguinal canal but lies outside the spermatic cord layers.
extraInfo: It provides sensory innervation to the skin of the medial thigh and the root of the penis/scrotum.

text: G cells are primarily located in the {{c1::gastric antrum}} and duodenum.
Parietal cells and Chief cells are primarily located in the {{c1::body and fundus}} of the stomach.
I cells, which secrete CCK, are located in the {{c1::duodenum and jejunum}}.
S cells, which secrete secretin, are located in the {{c1::duodenum}}.
K cells, which secrete GIP, are located in the {{c1::duodenum and jejunum}}.
Brunner glands are found in the {{c1::submucosa}} of the {{c2::duodenum}}.
D cells, which secrete somatostatin, are found in the {{c1::pancreatic islets}} and the GI mucosa.

topic: Pancreatic exocrine secretions and activation cascade
text: Enteropeptidase is a brush-border enzyme located in the {{c1::duodenal and jejunal}} mucosa.

topic: Pancreatic exocrine secretions and activation cascade
text: Trypsinogen is converted to its active form, trypsin, by the enzyme {{c1::enteropeptidase}}.

topic: Pancreatic exocrine secretions and activation cascade
text: Unlike the proteases, pancreatic {{c1::alpha-amylase::enzyme}} and {{c2::lipase::enzyme}} are secreted in their active forms.

topic: Pancreatic exocrine secretions and activation cascade
text: At high flow rates, the concentration of {{c1::bicarbonate}} in pancreatic juice increases, while the concentration of {{c2::chloride}} decreases.

topic: Pancreatic exocrine secretions and activation cascade
text: Pancreatic secretions are always {{c1::isotonic}} relative to plasma.

topic: Pancreatic exocrine secretions and activation cascade
text: The hormone {{c1::secretin}} stimulates pancreatic ductal cells to secrete a large volume of bicarbonate-rich fluid.

topic: Pancreatic exocrine secretions and activation cascade
text: Trypsin acts as a master activator by converting chymotrypsinogen to {{c1::chymotrypsin}}, proelastase to {{c2::elastase}}, and procarboxypeptidase to {{c3::carboxypeptidase}}.
Starch digestion begins in the mouth via {{c1::salivary alpha-amylase}}, which hydrolyzes {{c2::alpha-1,4}} glycosidic bonds.
extraInfo: Note that amylase cannot hydrolyze alpha-1,6 bonds or terminal alpha-1,4 bonds.

text: Glucose and galactose are absorbed at the apical membrane of enterocytes via the {{c1::SGLT1}} transporter, which utilizes {{c2::secondary active (sodium-dependent)}} transport.
extraInfo: This is why oral rehydration therapy contains both salt and sugar.

text: Fructose is absorbed at the apical membrane via {{c1::GLUT5}} through the mechanism of {{c2::facilitated diffusion}}.
extraInfo: Unlike glucose, fructose absorption is sodium-independent.

text: All monosaccharides (glucose, galactose, fructose) exit the basolateral membrane of enterocytes via the {{c1::GLUT2}} transporter.
extraInfo: GLUT2 is a facilitated diffusion transporter with a high capacity.

text: In lactase deficiency, colonic bacteria ferment undigested lactose, leading to {{c1::decreased}} stool pH and {{c2::increased}} breath hydrogen.
extraInfo: The acidic pH is due to the production of short-chain fatty acids like butyrate and acetate.

text: The {{c1::D-xylose}} absorption test is used to distinguish between pancreatic insufficiency and {{c2::mucosal malabsorption (e.g., Celiac disease)}}.
extraInfo: D-xylose is a monosaccharide that does not require pancreatic enzymes for digestion.

text: The enzyme {{c1::isomaltase}} is responsible for hydrolyzing the {{c2::alpha-1,6}} glycosidic bonds found at the branch points of alpha-limit dextrins.
extraInfo: Isomaltase is essential for the complete digestion of amylopectin and glycogen.

text: Peyer patches are unencapsulated lymphoid aggregates found primarily in the {{c1::lamina propria and submucosa}} of the {{c2::ileum}}.
{{c1::M (microfold)}} cells are specialized epithelial cells that sample intestinal antigens and transport them to underlying immune cells via {{c2::transcytosis}}.
B cells in Peyer patches undergo class switching to {{c1::IgA}} under the influence of {{c2::TGF-beta}} and IL-5.
Secretory IgA consists of two IgA monomers, one {{c1::J chain}}, and one {{c2::secretory component}} (derived from the pIgR).
The {{c1::secretory component}} protects secretory IgA from {{c2::proteolysis (degradation)}} by enzymes in the intestinal lumen.
Activated lymphocytes home back to the gut by expressing the integrin {{c1::alpha-4 beta-7}}, which binds to {{c2::MAdCAM-1}} on intestinal high endothelial venules.
Unlike lymph nodes, Peyer patches lack {{c1::afferent}} lymphatics and receive antigens directly from the intestinal lumen.
The rate-limiting enzyme in bile acid synthesis is {{c1::7α-hydroxylase}}.
The two primary bile acids synthesized in the liver are {{c1::cholic acid}} and {{c1::chenodeoxycholic acid}}.
The primary site of active bile acid reabsorption is the {{c1::terminal ileum}}.
Bile acids are conjugated with the amino acids {{c1::glycine}} or {{c1::taurine}} to increase their water solubility.
Secondary bile acids (deoxycholic and lithocholic acid) are formed by {{c1::bacterial dehydroxylation}} in the colon.
Bile acids facilitate the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, which include vitamins {{c1::A, D, E, and K}}.
Bile acid sequestrants like cholestyramine work by {{c1::interrupting the enterohepatic circulation}} of bile acids, leading to increased cholesterol consumption by the liver.
The primary site for iron absorption is the {{c1::duodenum}}.
Folate is absorbed in the {{c1::jejunum}}.
Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the {{c1::terminal ileum}}.
Iron is absorbed in the enterocytes in the {{c1::Fe2+ (ferrous)}} state.
Vitamin B12 absorption requires {{c1::Intrinsic Factor}}, which is secreted by {{c2::parietal}} cells in the stomach.
Bile acids are reabsorbed via the {{c1::terminal ileum}} as part of the enterohepatic circulation.
Vitamin B12 is released from haptocorrin (R-binder) in the {{c1::duodenum}} by the action of {{c2::pancreatic proteases}}.
Heme is converted to biliverdin by the enzyme {{c1::heme oxygenase}}.
The enzyme {{c1::UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1)}} is responsible for conjugating bilirubin with glucuronic acid.
Conjugated bilirubin is actively transported into the bile canaliculi by the {{c1::MRP2}} transporter.
Unconjugated bilirubin is {{c1::water-insoluble (lipophilic)}} and must be transported in the blood bound to {{c2::albumin}}.
The pigment responsible for the brown color of stool is {{c1::stercobilin}}, which is formed by the oxidation of {{c2::urobilinogen}}.
{{c1::Dubin-Johnson}} syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder featuring a defect in MRP2 and a characteristically {{c2::black}} liver.
In the kidney, urobilinogen is oxidized to {{c1::urobilin}}, which gives urine its yellow color.
The triad of Plummer-Vinson syndrome includes: {{c1::Dysphagia (esophageal webs)}}, {{c2::Iron deficiency anemia}}, and {{c3::Glossitis}}.
Boerhaave syndrome is a {{c1::transmural (full-thickness)}} rupture of the esophagus, whereas Mallory-Weiss syndrome is a {{c2::mucosal (partial-thickness)}} tear.
Barrett esophagus involves metaplasia of the distal esophagus from {{c1::nonkeratinized stratified squamous}} epithelium to {{c2::nonciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells}}.
In infectious esophagitis, {{c1::HSV-1}} is associated with punched-out ulcers, while {{c2::CMV}} is associated with linear ulcers.
The auscultation of a 'crunching' sound in the chest timed with the heartbeat (Hamman sign) is caused by {{c1::pneumomediastinum}}.
Diagnosis of eosinophilic esophagitis requires the presence of at least {{c1::15}} eosinophils per high-power field on biopsy.
Mallory-Weiss tears are typically {{c1::longitudinal}} lacerations located at the {{c2::gastroesophageal (GE) junction}}.
The most common salivary gland tumor is the {{c1::pleomorphic adenoma}}, which histologically contains both {{c2::epithelial}} and {{c3::mesenchymal}} (e.g., chondroid) tissues.
extraInfo: It is a benign 'mixed' tumor. High recurrence rate if not fully excised due to microscopic pseudopods.

text: Warthin tumor is a benign parotid tumor strongly associated with {{c1::smoking}} and characterized by {{c2::lymphoid germinal centers}} on histology.
extraInfo: Also called papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum. Often bilateral or multifocal.

text: The most common malignant salivary gland tumor is {{c1::mucoepidermoid carcinoma}}, which is composed of both {{c2::mucus-secreting}} and {{c3::squamous}} cells.
extraInfo: Often arises in the parotid; the most common salivary malignancy in children.

text: Salivary stones (sialolithiasis) most commonly occur in the {{c1::submandibular}} gland duct, also known as the {{c2::Wharton}} duct.
extraInfo: Presents with sudden-onset pain and swelling upon eating (postprandial).

text: Oral {{c1::leukoplakia}} is a white plaque that {{c2::cannot}} be scraped off and is considered a precancerous lesion.
extraInfo: Contrast with oral candidiasis (can be scraped off) and hairy leukoplakia (EBV-associated, non-precancerous).

text: Hairy leukoplakia is a non-precancerous white lesion on the {{c1::lateral tongue}} caused by the {{c2::Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)}} in immunocompromised patients.
extraInfo: Often a marker of progression in HIV/AIDS.

text: Compared to leukoplakia, {{c1::erythroplakia}} is associated with a significantly {{c2::higher}} risk of progression to squamous cell carcinoma.
extraInfo: Presents as a red, velvety plaque; often shows dysplasia or carcinoma in situ on biopsy.

text: Barrett esophagus is the replacement of {{c1::stratified squamous}} epithelium with {{c2::non-ciliated columnar}} epithelium.
extraInfo: This is a form of intestinal metaplasia often containing goblet cells.

text: The diagnostic histological hallmark of Barrett esophagus is the presence of {{c1::goblet cells}} in the esophageal mucosa.
extraInfo: Goblet cells are mucus-secreting cells normally found in the intestines.

text: Barrett esophagus is a specialized type of metaplasia that occurs due to chronic {{c1::GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease)}}.
extraInfo: The change in cell type is an adaptation to handle the low pH of gastric acid.

text: A major clinical concern in Barrett esophagus is the increased risk of developing {{c1::esophageal adenocarcinoma}}.
extraInfo: Squamous cell carcinoma is the other main type of esophageal cancer but is not typically caused by Barrett.

text: Metaplasia in Barrett esophagus arises from the {{c1::reprogramming of stem cells}} rather than the transformation of mature cells.
extraInfo: This is a key principle: metaplasia involves a change in the differentiation pathway of precursor cells.

text: The progression of cellular changes in the distal esophagus is: Metaplasia → {{c1::Dysplasia}} → Adenocarcinoma.
extraInfo: Dysplasia is the disordered, precancerous stage.

text: Unlike metaplasia, {{c1::dysplasia}} is characterized by a loss of tissue orientation and nuclear pleomorphism.
extraInfo: Metaplasia consists of normal-appearing cells in an abnormal location, whereas dysplasia consists of abnormal-appearing cells.

text: Achalasia is caused by the loss of {{c1::ganglion cells}} in the {{c2::myenteric (Auerbach)}} plexus.
The two primary inhibitory neurotransmitters that are deficient in the lower esophageal sphincter in achalasia are {{c1::nitric oxide (NO)}} and {{c2::vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)}}.
Esophageal manometry in achalasia typically shows {{c1::incomplete LES relaxation}}, {{c2::high resting LES pressure}}, and {{c3::aperistalsis}}.
The classic finding for achalasia on barium swallow is the {{c1::bird's beak}} sign.
Secondary achalasia can be caused by the parasite {{c1::Trypanosoma cruzi}}, which is the causative agent of {{c2::Chagas disease}}.
Unlike scleroderma, which has {{c1::low}} LES pressure, achalasia is characterized by {{c2::high}} LES pressure.
Chronic stasis of food in achalasia increases the long-term risk of developing {{c1::squamous cell carcinoma}} of the esophagus.
The most common type of esophageal cancer in the United States is {{c1::adenocarcinoma}}, whereas the most common worldwide is {{c2::squamous cell carcinoma}}.
extraInfo: Adenocarcinoma is linked to GERD/Barrett's; SCC is linked to smoking/alcohol/caustic injury.

text: Esophageal adenocarcinoma typically arises in the {{c1::lower (distal) one-third}} of the esophagus.
extraInfo: This corresponds with the area most affected by acid reflux and Barrett metaplasia.

text: Barrett esophagus involves metaplasia of stratified squamous epithelium to {{c1::nonciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells}}.
extraInfo: Goblet cells are the key marker of 'intestinal metaplasia'.

text: Lymphatic drainage for the middle third of the esophagus is to the {{c1::mediastinal}} or {{c2::tracheobronchial}} lymph nodes.
extraInfo: Upper third drains to cervical; lower third drains to celiac/gastric nodes.

text: The triad of Plummer-Vinson syndrome includes {{c1::dysphagia (esophageal webs)}}, {{c2::iron deficiency anemia}}, and {{c3::glossitis}}.
extraInfo: This syndrome carries an increased risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

text: Esophageal cancer classically presents with progressive dysphagia, starting with {{c1::solids}} and eventually progressing to {{c2::liquids}}.
extraInfo: This contrasts with achalasia, where dysphagia to both solids and liquids often occurs simultaneously.

text: Chronic food stasis in {{c1::achalasia}} increases the risk of developing {{c2::squamous cell carcinoma}}.
extraInfo: This is due to chronic irritation of the squamous lining.

text: The intestinal type of gastric adenocarcinoma is strongly associated with {{c1::H. pylori}} infection.
extraInfo: This type is also associated with smoking, nitrosamines (smoked foods), and chronic atrophic gastritis.

text: {{c1::Signet ring}} cells are the characteristic histological finding in the diffuse type of gastric adenocarcinoma.
extraInfo: These cells contain intracellular mucin that pushes the nucleus to the periphery.

text: A {{c1::Krukenberg}} tumor is a signet ring cell adenocarcinoma that has metastasized to the ovaries.
extraInfo: It is often bilateral and usually originates from a gastric primary.

text: Gastric adenocarcinoma is most commonly associated with Blood Group {{c1::A}}.
extraInfo: In contrast, Blood Group O is associated with duodenal ulcers.

text: The {{c1::Virchow}} node is a left supraclavicular lymph node that indicates metastatic spread from an abdominal malignancy.
extraInfo: Troisier's sign is the clinical finding of this enlarged node.

text: Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma is often caused by a mutation in the {{c1::CDH1 (or E-cadherin)}} gene.
extraInfo: This mutation leads to loss of cell-cell adhesion and the characteristic linitis plastica (leather bottle stomach).

text: The sudden onset of multiple seborrheic keratoses, known as the {{c1::Leser-Trélat}} sign, is a paraneoplastic syndrome of gastric cancer.
extraInfo: It is thought to be mediated by the release of transforming growth factor-alpha (TGF-alpha).

topic: Gastritis (Acute vs Chronic) and Ménétrier disease
text: Curling ulcers are associated with {{c1::severe burns}}, which lead to mucosal {{c2::ischemia}} and erosion.
extraInfo: The hypovolemia from burns decreases blood flow to the stomach, weakening the mucosal barrier.

topic: Gastritis (Acute vs Chronic) and Ménétrier disease
text: Cushing ulcers result from increased {{c1::intracranial pressure}}, which stimulates the {{c2::vagus nerve}} to increase gastric {{c3::acid (HCl)}} production.
extraInfo: Vagal stimulation increases acetylcholine, which directly acts on parietal cell M3 receptors.

topic: Gastritis (Acute vs Chronic) and Ménétrier disease
text: Chronic Gastritis Type A (Autoimmune) primarily affects the {{c1::body and fundus}} of the stomach and is associated with {{c2::pernicious anemia}}.
extraInfo: It involves antibodies against parietal cells and intrinsic factor.

topic: Gastritis (Acute vs Chronic) and Ménétrier disease
text: Chronic Gastritis Type B is caused by {{c1::Helicobacter pylori}} and usually starts in the {{c2::antrum}}.
extraInfo: Type B is the most common cause of chronic gastritis and increases risk for MALT lymphoma and adenocarcinoma.

topic: Gastritis (Acute vs Chronic) and Ménétrier disease
text: Ménétrier disease is characterized by excess production of {{c1::TGF-alpha}}, leading to {{c2::foveolar (mucous cell)}} hyperplasia.
extraInfo: This gives the stomach a 'brain-like' appearance with giant rugal folds.

topic: Gastritis (Acute vs Chronic) and Ménétrier disease
text: In autoimmune gastritis, the destruction of parietal cells leads to a loss of negative feedback, causing {{c1::hypergastrinemia}} and {{c2::G-cell}} hyperplasia.
extraInfo: The lack of acid (achlorhydria) means there is no inhibition of gastrin release.

topic: Gastritis (Acute vs Chronic) and Ménétrier disease
text: Ménétrier disease is a {{c1::protein}}-losing enteropathy, which often manifests clinically as {{c2::peripheral edema}}.
extraInfo: Loss of albumin through the hypertrophied gastric mucosa decreases plasma oncotic pressure.

topic: Peptic ulcer disease (Gastric vs Duodenal ulcers)
text: Duodenal ulcer pain {{c1::decreases}} with meals, which can lead to {{c2::weight gain}}.

topic: Peptic ulcer disease (Gastric vs Duodenal ulcers)
text: Gastric ulcer pain {{c1::increases}} with meals, which can lead to {{c2::weight loss}}.

topic: Peptic ulcer disease (Gastric vs Duodenal ulcers)
text: The most common vessel involved in a bleeding posterior duodenal ulcer is the {{c1::gastroduodenal artery}}.

topic: Peptic ulcer disease (Gastric vs Duodenal ulcers)
text: Unlike duodenal ulcers, gastric ulcers carry an increased risk of {{c1::malignancy (adenocarcinoma)}} and must be {{c2::biopsied}}.

topic: Peptic ulcer disease (Gastric vs Duodenal ulcers)
text: H. pylori-induced duodenal ulcers are associated with {{c1::increased}} gastric acid secretion due to destruction of {{c2::D cells (somatostatin)}} in the antrum.

topic: Peptic ulcer disease (Gastric vs Duodenal ulcers)
text: Anterior duodenal ulcers are more likely to {{c1::perforate}}, while posterior duodenal ulcers are more likely to {{c2::bleed}}.

topic: Peptic ulcer disease (Gastric vs Duodenal ulcers)
text: Gastric ulcers are most commonly located on the {{c1::lesser curvature}} and are often associated with erosion of the {{c2::left gastric artery}}.
The anatomical boundary between upper and lower gastrointestinal bleeding is the {{c1::ligament of Treitz}} (or {{c1::suspensory muscle of the duodenum}}).
An elevated BUN-to-creatinine ratio (typically {{c1::>20:1}} or {{c1::30:1}}) in the context of GI bleeding strongly suggests an {{c2::upper}} GI source.
The most common cause of significant upper gastrointestinal bleeding is {{c1::peptic ulcer disease}}.
In patients with lower GI bleeding, the most common cause of massive, painless hematochezia in the elderly is {{c1::diverticulosis}}.
Meckel diverticulum causes painless hematochezia in children due to the presence of {{c1::ectopic gastric mucosa}}, which secretes acid and ulcers the ileum.
{{c1::Angiodysplasia::Diagnosis}} is a cause of episodic lower GI bleeding associated with {{c2::aortic stenosis::cardiac condition}} (Heyde syndrome).
A patient with hematochezia and hemodynamic instability should first have an {{c1::upper}} GI source ruled out, often via {{c2::nasogastric lavage}} or {{c2::EGD}}.
Celiac disease is an autoimmune-mediated intolerance to {{c1::gliadin}}, a component of gluten.
extraInfo: It is associated with HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8.

text: The classic histological findings in Celiac disease are {{c1::villous atrophy}}, {{c2::crypt hyperplasia}}, and {{c3::intraepithelial lymphocytosis}}.
extraInfo: These changes occur primarily in the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum.

text: Whipple disease is caused by the Gram-positive rod {{c1::Tropheryma whipplei}}.
extraInfo: It is most common in older males.

text: The histological hallmark of Whipple disease is the presence of {{c1::PAS-positive}} foamy macrophages in the {{c2::lamina propria}}.
extraInfo: The PAS-positive granules represent partially digested bacterial cell walls.

text: Unlike Celiac disease, Tropical sprue can affect the {{c1::distal ileum}}, frequently leading to {{c2::Vitamin B12}} deficiency.
extraInfo: It also commonly causes folate deficiency and responds to antibiotics.

text: In the D-xylose test, urinary excretion is {{c1::decreased}} in mucosal diseases (e.g., Celiac) but {{c2::normal}} in pancreatic insufficiency.
extraInfo: D-xylose is a monosaccharide that does not require pancreatic enzymes for absorption.

text: Dermatitis herpetiformis is a pruritic, vesicular skin rash associated with Celiac disease characterized by {{c1::IgA}} deposits at the {{c2::tips of dermal papillae}}.
extraInfo: It is treated with a gluten-free diet and Dapsone.

text: The medications {{c1::hyoscyamine}} and {{c1::dicyclomine}} are used as antispasmodics in the treatment of irritable bowel syndrome.
extraInfo: They belong to the muscarinic antagonist drug class.

text: Dicyclomine treats IBS by acting as a(n) {{c1::antagonist}} at {{c2::muscarinic (M3)}} receptors in the gastrointestinal tract.
extraInfo: This leads to smooth muscle relaxation and decreased motility.

text: The use of muscarinic antagonists for IBS is contraindicated in patients with {{c1::acute angle-closure glaucoma}} due to the risk of mydriasis.
extraInfo: Mydriasis can further narrow the iridocorneal angle.

text: A common genitourinary side effect of hyoscyamine is {{c1::urinary retention}}, making it risky for patients with {{c2::benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)}}.
extraInfo: Antimuscarinics relax the detrusor muscle, preventing bladder emptying.

text: Muscarinic antagonists like dicyclomine cause {{c1::tachycardia}} by blocking {{c2::M2}} receptors in the sinoatrial node.
extraInfo: This removes the inhibitory vagal tone on the heart.

text: Antispasmodics can cause hyperthermia (the 'Hot as a hare' effect) by inhibiting {{c1::eccrine}} sweat glands.
extraInfo: These glands are innervated by sympathetic cholinergic fibers.

text: The ocular side effect of hyoscyamine that causes blurred near vision is called {{c1::cycloplegia}}, which is the paralysis of the {{c2::ciliary}} muscle.
extraInfo: This prevents the lens from changing shape to focus on close objects.

text: Microscopic colitis typically causes chronic {{c1::watery}} diarrhea.
extraInfo: The diarrhea is non-bloody and often secretory in nature.

text: In microscopic colitis, the colonic mucosa appears grossly {{c1::normal}} on endoscopy.
extraInfo: This is why biopsies are essential for diagnosis.

text: The demographic most commonly affected by microscopic colitis is {{c1::older females}}.
extraInfo: It is a frequent cause of chronic diarrhea in the geriatric population.

text: Lymphocytic colitis is characterized histologically by an increase in {{c1::intraepithelial lymphocytes}}.
extraInfo: This occurs in the surface epithelium of the colon.

text: Collagenous colitis is characterized by a thickened {{c1::subepithelial collagen band}}.
extraInfo: The band is typically >10 micrometers in thickness.

text: Unlike IBS, microscopic colitis is an {{c1::inflammatory}} disease of the colon.
extraInfo: Markers like fecal calprotectin may be elevated.

text: The inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria of microscopic colitis consists primarily of {{c1::lymphocytes}}.
extraInfo: Plasma cells may also be present, but the lymphocytic increase is the hallmark.

text: The most common cause of appendicitis in adults is a {{c1::fecalith}}.
extraInfo: In contrast, lymphoid hyperplasia is the most common cause in children.

text: Early appendicitis pain is referred to the {{c1::T10}} dermatome due to visceral afferent fibers.
extraInfo: This is why pain starts in the periumbilical region before migrating to the RLQ.

text: The landmark for the appendix base is the convergence of the {{c1::taeniae coli}} on the cecum.
extraInfo: This is a critical surgical landmark during appendectomy.

text: The {{c1::Psoas}} sign is elicited by extending the right hip and suggests a {{c2::retrocecal}} appendix.
extraInfo: This position is the most common anatomical variation of the appendix tip.

text: The definitive histological diagnosis of acute appendicitis requires {{c1::neutrophils}} in the {{c2::muscularis propria}}.
extraInfo: Mucosal inflammation alone is insufficient for the diagnosis.

text: {{c1::Yersinia enterocolitica}} is the classic organism that causes pseudoappendicitis through {{c2::mesenteric adenitis}}.
extraInfo: It is often transmitted via contaminated pork products or pet feces.

text: In pregnant patients, the appendix is displaced {{c1::superiorly (or toward the RUQ)}} by the gravid uterus.
extraInfo: This makes the diagnosis challenging as it deviates from McBurney's point tenderness.

topic: Inflammatory bowel diseases (Crohn disease vs Ulcerative colitis)
text: The anatomical distribution of Crohn disease is characterized by {{c1::skip lesions::type of lesion distribution}} and {{c2::rectal sparing::rectal involvement status}}.

topic: Inflammatory bowel diseases (Crohn disease vs Ulcerative colitis)
text: Ulcerative colitis is always associated with {{c1::continuous}} involvement of the {{c2::rectum}}.

topic: Inflammatory bowel diseases (Crohn disease vs Ulcerative colitis)
text: Microscopically, Crohn disease is distinguished by {{c1::noncaseating granulomas::specific inflammatory finding}} and {{c2::transmural}} inflammation.

topic: Inflammatory bowel diseases (Crohn disease vs Ulcerative colitis)
text: The microscopic hallmark of Ulcerative Colitis is the presence of {{c1::crypt abscesses}} and ulcers in the {{c2::mucosa and submucosa::layers of the bowel wall}}.

topic: Inflammatory bowel diseases (Crohn disease vs Ulcerative colitis)
text: {{c1::Cigarette smoking}} is a risk factor for Crohn disease but is {{c2::protective}} against Ulcerative Colitis.

topic: Inflammatory bowel diseases (Crohn disease vs Ulcerative colitis)
text: The radiologic sign 'string sign' is associated with {{c1::Crohn disease}}, while the 'lead pipe' appearance is associated with {{c2::Ulcerative Colitis}}.

topic: Inflammatory bowel diseases (Crohn disease vs Ulcerative colitis)
text: A common hepatobiliary complication of Ulcerative Colitis is {{c1::Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)}}, which is often associated with the serologic marker {{c2::p-ANCA}}.
The most common location for colonic diverticula is the {{c1::sigmoid colon}}.
extraInfo: This is due to the smaller radius and higher intraluminal pressure in this segment.

text: Diverticulosis consists of {{c1::false}} diverticula, which contain only the {{c2::mucosa}} and {{c2::submucosa}} layers.
extraInfo: They lack the muscularis propria.

text: Diverticular bleeding occurs due to mechanical erosion of the {{c1::vasa recta}}.
extraInfo: These vessels penetrate the muscularis and become stretched over the diverticular sac.

text: The imaging modality of choice for suspected acute diverticulitis is {{c1::CT scan (with contrast)}}.
extraInfo: Colonoscopy and barium enema are contraindicated in the acute phase due to perforation risk.

text: A colovesical fistula typically presents with {{c1::pneumaturia}} or {{c1::fecaluria}}.
extraInfo: It results from an inflammatory connection between the colon and the bladder.

text: Diverticular bleeding is classically {{c1::painless}} hematochezia.
extraInfo: In contrast, bleeding in diverticulitis is rare; diverticulitis presents with LLQ pain.

text: The primary dietary recommendation to prevent diverticulosis is a {{c1::high-fiber}} diet.
extraInfo: Fiber increases stool bulk and decreases the pressure required for defecation.

text: Meckel diverticulum is a remnant of the {{c1::vitelline (omphalomesenteric)}} duct.
extraInfo: This duct normally connects the midgut to the yolk sac.

text: The 'Rule of 2s' states that Meckel diverticulum is located {{c1::2 feet}} proximal to the ileocecal valve.
extraInfo: It is also roughly 2 inches long and 2% of the population is affected.

text: Meckel diverticulum is a {{c1::true}} diverticulum because it contains {{c2::all three}} layers of the bowel wall.
extraInfo: Layers: mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis propria.

text: The most common ectopic tissue found in Meckel diverticulum is {{c1::gastric mucosa}}.
extraInfo: The second most common is pancreatic tissue.

text: The diagnostic test of choice for Meckel diverticulum presenting with bleeding is a {{c1::Technetium-99m pertechnetate}} scan.
extraInfo: This is also called a 'Meckel scan'; the tracer is taken up by ectopic gastric mucosa.

text: Meckel diverticulum occurs on the {{c1::antimesenteric}} border of the ileum.
extraInfo: This helps differentiate it from duplications which occur on the mesenteric border.

text: The most common clinical presentation of Meckel diverticulum in children is {{c1::painless hematochezia}}.
extraInfo: It may also present as intussusception, volvulus, or diverticulitis (mimicking appendicitis).

text: Hirschsprung disease is caused by the failure of {{c1::neural crest}} cells to migrate {{c2::caudally}} during development.
extraInfo: Migration usually completes by week 12. Failure results in a lack of ganglion cells in the distal colon.

text: In Hirschsprung disease, the histological hallmark is the absence of the {{c1::Meissner (submucosal)}} and {{c2::Auerbach (myenteric)}} plexuses.
extraInfo: The Meissner plexus controls secretion/blood flow, while the Auerbach plexus controls motility.

text: The segment of the colon that is always involved in Hirschsprung disease is the {{c1::rectum}}.
extraInfo: Because migration is cranial-to-caudal, the most distal part is always affected if migration is interrupted.

text: A classic clinical sign of Hirschsprung disease during a digital rectal exam is the {{c1::squirt (or blast)}} sign.
extraInfo: This is the explosive release of gas and stool upon withdrawal of the finger, caused by the relief of the functional obstruction.

text: Hirschsprung disease is associated with a loss-of-function mutation in the {{c1::RET}} proto-oncogene.
extraInfo: Conversely, gain-of-function RET mutations are associated with MEN 2A and MEN 2B.

text: The definitive gold-standard diagnostic test for Hirschsprung disease is {{c1::rectal suction biopsy}}.
extraInfo: It must contain submucosa to evaluate for the presence or absence of ganglion cells.

text: Hirschsprung disease is highly associated with the chromosomal abnormality {{c1::Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)}}.
extraInfo: Approximately 10% of patients with Hirschsprung have Down syndrome.

text: The most common site for pediatric intussusception is the {{c1::ileocecal}} junction.
extraInfo: This is often triggered by lymphoid hyperplasia (Peyer's patches) following a viral infection like Adenovirus.

text: The classic clinical triad of intussusception includes {{c1::intermittent abdominal pain}}, a {{c2::sausage-shaped mass}}, and {{c3::currant jelly stools}}.
extraInfo: The currant jelly appearance is due to a mixture of blood and mucus from venous congestion.

text: The preferred initial imaging modality to diagnose intussusception is {{c1::ultrasound}}, which shows a pathognomonic {{c2::target (or donut)}} sign.
extraInfo: The target sign represents concentric loops of bowel in cross-section.

text: In adults, intussusception is usually caused by a structural lead point, most commonly {{c1::malignancy (or a tumor)}}.
extraInfo: In contrast, most pediatric cases are idiopathic or caused by lymphoid hyperplasia.

text: The two major contraindications for the rotavirus vaccine are a history of {{c1::intussusception}} and the immunodeficiency {{c2::SCID}}.
extraInfo: The vaccine is live-attenuated and has been associated with a small risk of triggering bowel telescoping.

text: The therapeutic procedure of choice for stable pediatric intussusception is an {{c1::air (pneumatic)}} or {{c2::contrast (hydrostatic)}} enema.
extraInfo: If the enema fails or there are signs of peritonitis/perforation, surgical reduction is required.

text: In intussusception, the {{c1::intussusceptum}} is the proximal segment that telescopes into the distal {{c2::intussuscipiens}}.
extraInfo: Mnemonic help: The intussusceptum 'enters', and the intussuscipiens 'receives' (like a recipient).

text: In short bowel syndrome, the loss of the {{c1::distal ileum}} prevents the reabsorption of bile salts.
extraInfo: The distal ileum contains specific transporters for the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids.

text: Fat malabsorption in SBS leads to calcium binding to {{c1::fatty acids/fats}}, which leaves {{c2::oxalate}} free to be absorbed.
extraInfo: This mechanism results in enteric hyperoxaluria and calcium oxalate kidney stones.

text: The rate-limiting enzyme in bile acid synthesis is {{c1::Cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase}}.
extraInfo: This enzyme is found in the liver and is inhibited by the return of bile acids via the portal vein.

text: Bile acids are conjugated to {{c1::glycine}} or {{c1::taurine}} to form water-soluble bile salts.
extraInfo: Conjugation lowers the pKa of the bile acid, ensuring it remains ionized and effective as a detergent in the small intestine.

text: Bacterial metabolism of bilirubin in the gut produces {{c1::urobilinogen}}, which is then oxidized to {{c2::stercobilin}} in the feces.
extraInfo: Stercobilin is the pigment responsible for the brown color of stool.

text: Heme is first converted to the green pigment {{c1::biliverdin}} by the enzyme {{c2::heme oxygenase}}.
extraInfo: This reaction also releases iron (Fe2+) and carbon monoxide (CO).

text: Bile salts provide antimicrobial activity through the disruption of {{c1::bacterial cell membranes}}.
extraInfo: Loss of bile salts in SBS can lead to small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO).

text: The hallmark clinical presentation of early acute mesenteric ischemia is {{c1::pain out of proportion to physical exam findings}}.
Chronic mesenteric ischemia, also known as 'intestinal angina,' is most commonly caused by {{c1::atherosclerosis}} and presents as {{c2::postprandial}} abdominal pain.
The most common site for ischemic colitis is the {{c1::splenic flexure}}, which is a watershed area between the {{c2::SMA::artery}} and the {{c3::IMA::artery}}.
In the setting of bowel ischemia, {{c1::thumbprinting}} on imaging represents {{c2::submucosal edema or hemorrhage}}.
The most common underlying cardiac condition leading to an embolic acute mesenteric ischemia is {{c1::atrial fibrillation}}.
Symptomatic chronic mesenteric ischemia typically requires significant narrowing of at least {{c1::two}} of the three major mesenteric arteries.
The finding of {{c1::pneumatosis intestinalis}} (gas in the bowel wall) on CT scan suggests {{c2::transmural infarction/necrosis}}.
The most common cause of small bowel obstruction (SBO) in adults with a history of abdominal surgery is {{c1::postoperative adhesions}}.
A classic radiographic finding of mechanical small bowel obstruction is {{c1::multiple air-fluid levels}} on an upright X-ray.
The most common site of impaction for a gallstone in gallstone ileus is the {{c1::ileocecal valve}}.
In a paralytic ileus, bowel sounds are typically {{c1::absent}} or {{c2::decreased}}, whereas in early SBO they are {{c3::high-pitched/tinkling}}.
The electrolyte abnormality most frequently associated with paralytic ileus is {{c1::hypokalemia}}.
Obstipation is defined as the inability to pass {{c1::stool}} and {{c2::flatus}}.
The radiographic presence of air in the biliary tree, known as {{c1::pneumobilia}}, is a component of Rigler's triad in gallstone ileus.
The two most common 'watershed' areas susceptible to colonic ischemia are the {{c1::splenic flexure}} (Griffith point) and the {{c2::rectosigmoid junction}} (Sudeck point).
extraInfo: These areas are located at the distal reaches of the SMA/IMA and IMA/Superior rectal artery supplies, respectively.

text: Angiodysplasia most commonly occurs in the {{c1::cecum}} and right colon due to the {{c2::Law of Laplace}}, which states that wall tension is highest in segments with the largest diameter.
extraInfo: The cecum has the largest radius of the entire colon.

text: Heyde syndrome is characterized by the triad of {{c1::aortic stenosis}}, acquired {{c2::von Willebrand disease}} (loss of high-molecular-weight multimers), and bleeding from {{c3::angiodysplasia}}.
extraInfo: Shear stress across the stenotic valve destroys the vWF multimers.

text: Ischemic colitis classically presents with crampy abdominal pain followed by {{c1::hematochezia (bloody diarrhea)}} and is often seen in the elderly or after {{c2::AAA repair}}.
extraInfo: IMA ligation during AAA repair is a high-yield surgical cause.

text: The classic radiographic finding of colonic ischemia on plain film or CT is {{c1::thumbprinting}}, which represents {{c2::submucosal edema and hemorrhage}}.
extraInfo: This is seen as rounded indentations into the colonic lumen.

text: In most cases of colonic ischemia, the {{c1::rectum}} is spared because it has a dual blood supply from the {{c2::IMA}} and the {{c3::internal iliac}} arteries.
extraInfo: The middle and inferior rectal arteries arise from the internal iliac system.

text: Angiodysplasia is characterized histologically by {{c1::ectatic (dilated)}}, tortuous vessels in the {{c2::mucosa and submucosa}}.
extraInfo: They are acquired vascular malformations, not true neoplasms.

text: The most significant risk factor for necrotizing enterocolitis is {{c1::prematurity}} (or low birth weight).
extraInfo: NEC is inversely proportional to gestational age and birth weight.

text: The pathognomonic radiographic finding for necrotizing enterocolitis is {{c1::pneumatosis intestinalis}}.
extraInfo: This represents gas produced by bacteria within the bowel wall.

text: The absolute radiographic indication for surgery in necrotizing enterocolitis is {{c1::pneumoperitoneum}}.
extraInfo: Pneumoperitoneum indicates intestinal perforation.

text: In infants who recover from NEC, the most common long-term complication is {{c1::intestinal stricture}}.
extraInfo: Strictures result from fibrosis during the healing of the necrotic bowel wall.

text: {{c1::Breast milk}} is a protective factor that reduces the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm infants.
extraInfo: Breast milk contains IgA and other factors that support mucosal immunity.

text: Necrotizing enterocolitis most commonly affects the {{c1::terminal ileum}} and proximal colon.
extraInfo: These areas are particularly susceptible to ischemic injury and bacterial translocation.

text: Radiographic visualization of air in the {{c1::portal vein}} is a sign of severe necrotizing enterocolitis.
extraInfo: Portal venous gas signifies that intramural air has entered the mesenteric venous drainage.

text: The {{c1::APC}} gene is located on chromosome {{c2::5q21}}.
In the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, mutation of the {{c1::KRAS}} gene leads to the growth of the polyp from a small to a large adenoma.
Gardner syndrome is characterized by Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) plus {{c1::osteomas}} and {{c2::soft tissue tumors (e.g., epidermal cysts, desmoid tumors)}}.
Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) is caused by a germline mutation in {{c1::DNA mismatch repair}} genes, such as {{c2::MLH1 or MSH2}}.
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is associated with an increased risk of colorectal, {{c1::breast}}, and {{c2::pancreatic}} cancers.
{{c1::Villous}} adenomas have a higher risk of malignant transformation than tubular adenomas.
The two types of CNS tumors associated with Turcot syndrome are {{c1::medulloblastoma}} (APC variant) and {{c2::glioma/glioblastoma}} (Lynch variant).
In the pathogenesis of cirrhosis, hepatic {{c1::stellate (Ito)}} cells are activated to produce {{c2::collagen}}, leading to fibrosis.
Esophageal varices result from an anastomosis between the {{c1::left gastric}} vein (portal) and the {{c2::azygos/esophageal}} veins (systemic).
A Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) of {{c1::≥ 1.1}} g/dL indicates that the ascites is caused by {{c2::portal hypertension}}.
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is diagnosed when the ascitic fluid neutrophil count is greater than {{c1::250}} cells/mm³.
In hepatic encephalopathy, excess ammonia is converted to {{c1::glutamine}} within {{c2::astrocytes}}, causing osmotic swelling.
Anorectal varices are caused by an anastomosis between the {{c1::superior rectal}} vein and the {{c2::middle/inferior rectal}} veins.
Physical findings like spider angiomata and gynecomastia in cirrhosis are caused by {{c1::hyperestrogenism}} due to decreased hepatic metabolism.
Lynch syndrome is caused by a germline mutation in genes responsible for {{c1::DNA mismatch repair (MMR)}}.
The DNA mismatch repair mechanism is most active during the {{c1::S}} phase of the cell cycle.
The molecular hallmark of tumors in Lynch syndrome is {{c1::microsatellite instability (MSI)}}.
The two genes most commonly mutated in Lynch syndrome are {{c1::MLH1}} and {{c2::MSH2}}.
In Lynch syndrome, colorectal cancers are most frequently found in the {{c1::proximal (or right-sided)}} colon.
The most common extracolonic malignancy associated with Lynch syndrome is {{c1::endometrial carcinoma}}.
Lynch syndrome follows an {{c1::autosomal dominant}} pattern of inheritance.
In the chromosomal instability pathway of colorectal cancer, the sequence of mutations is {{c1::APC}}, then {{c2::KRAS}}, and finally {{c3::p53/SMAD4}}.
extraInfo: This is also known as the Vogelstein or adenoma-carcinoma sequence.

text: The APC gene is located on chromosome {{c1::5q21}}.
extraInfo: FAP is caused by a germline mutation in this gene.

text: Right-sided colorectal cancers are more likely to present with {{c1::iron deficiency anemia (or occult bleeding)}}, while left-sided cancers often present with {{c2::bowel obstruction (or altered bowel habits)}}.
extraInfo: Right-sided = ascending; Left-sided = descending/sigmoid.

text: Lynch syndrome is caused by a germline mutation in {{c1::DNA mismatch repair (MMR)}} genes.
extraInfo: The genes involved are MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2.

text: The finding of bacteremia or endocarditis caused by {{c1::Streptococcus bovis (S. gallolyticus)}} should prompt a search for hidden colonic malignancy.
extraInfo: This organism is a Group D streptococcus.

text: A circumferential, constricting lesion of the descending colon is described as an {{c1::apple-core}} lesion on barium enema.
extraInfo: This corresponds to the clinical 'napkin-ring' appearance.

text: Among adenomatous polyps, the {{c1::villous}} histological type carries the highest risk of malignant transformation.
extraInfo: Mnemonic-free fact: 'Villous is the Villain' describes the high risk.

topic: Budd-Chiari syndrome vs Portal vein thrombosis
text: Budd-Chiari syndrome is caused by the obstruction of {{c1::hepatic venous outflow}}.

topic: Budd-Chiari syndrome vs Portal vein thrombosis
text: The classic histological finding in Budd-Chiari syndrome is {{c1::centrilobular (Zone 3)}} congestion.

topic: Budd-Chiari syndrome vs Portal vein thrombosis
text: In contrast to right heart failure, Budd-Chiari syndrome usually presents with a {{c1::normal::normal/elevated}} jugular venous pressure (JVP).

topic: Budd-Chiari syndrome vs Portal vein thrombosis
text: Isolated portal vein thrombosis typically presents with portal hypertension signs (like varices) but WITHOUT {{c1::ascites}}.

topic: Budd-Chiari syndrome vs Portal vein thrombosis
text: Chronic portal vein thrombosis is associated with the formation of collateral vessels known as {{c1::cavernous transformation}}.

topic: Budd-Chiari syndrome vs Portal vein thrombosis
text: The triad of abdominal pain, ascites, and hepatomegaly is characteristic of {{c1::Budd-Chiari syndrome}}.

topic: Budd-Chiari syndrome vs Portal vein thrombosis
text: {{c1::Polycythemia vera}} is the most common myeloproliferative disorder associated with Budd-Chiari syndrome.

topic: Serum biochemical markers of liver injury and function
text: In alcoholic liver disease, the ratio of AST to ALT is typically {{c1::> 2:1}}.

topic: Serum biochemical markers of liver injury and function
text: The enzyme {{c1::gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT)}} is used to confirm that an elevated alkaline phosphatase is of hepatic rather than bony origin.

topic: Serum biochemical markers of liver injury and function
text: The most sensitive marker for acute changes in liver synthetic function is {{c1::Prothrombin Time (PT)}}.

topic: Serum biochemical markers of liver injury and function
text: {{c1::Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)}} is more specific for liver injury than AST because AST is also found in heart and skeletal muscle.

topic: Serum biochemical markers of liver injury and function
text: In most forms of hepatocellular injury (excluding alcohol), the ratio of transaminases typically shows {{c1::ALT > AST}}.

topic: Serum biochemical markers of liver injury and function
text: The neurotoxin primarily responsible for hepatic encephalopathy in liver failure is {{c1::ammonia}}.

topic: Serum biochemical markers of liver injury and function
text: {{c1::Albumin}} is a marker of liver synthetic function with a long half-life (approx. 20 days), making it more useful for chronic rather than acute assessment.
Reye syndrome is associated with viral infections, specifically {{c1::VZV (Varicella)}} and {{c1::influenza}}, that have been treated with {{c2::aspirin (salicylates)}}.
extraInfo: The only exception for aspirin use in children is Kawasaki disease.

text: The primary pathophysiologic mechanism of Reye syndrome is the reversible inhibition of {{c1::mitochondrial enzymes}} by aspirin metabolites, leading to impaired {{c2::β-oxidation}}.
extraInfo: This mitochondrial hit results in systemic metabolic failure.

text: The classic liver biopsy finding in Reye syndrome is {{c1::microvesicular fatty change (steatosis)}}.
